name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
summary: Persistent, impairing inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity beginning in childhood. FDA-approved options are methylphenidate- and amphetamine-based CNS stimulants (Schedule II), the norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors atomoxetine and viloxazine, the extended-release alpha-2 agonists guanfacine and clonidine, and (approved July 2026, DEA scheduling pending) the triple reuptake inhibitor centanafadine. Since 2023 all stimulant labels carry a unified boxed warning on abuse, misuse, and addiction. In 2025 FDA added a Limitation of Use to extended-release stimulant labels: use is not recommended under age 6 because of higher drug exposure and adverse reactions such as weight loss.
plainSummary: ADHD makes it hard to pay attention, sit still, or control impulses, and it often starts in childhood and can last into adulthood. Several types of medicine can help, including stimulants and non-stimulants, and doctors pick one based on age, other health issues, and side effects.

offLabel.use: ADHD in preschool-aged children when behavioral treatment is insufficient
offLabel.notes: Methylphenidate products are not labeled for children under 6, and 2025 labeling states extended-release stimulants are not recommended under 6 because of higher exposure and weight loss. The AAP guideline places parent training in behavior management first and allows methylphenidate for moderate-to-severe persistent impairment; the PATS trial supports efficacy at low IR doses, with more adverse effects than in older children. Amphetamine IR products are labeled from age 3.

references.label: Wolraich ML et al. AAP clinical practice guideline for ADHD. Pediatrics 2019 (PMID 31570648)
Greenhill L et al. Efficacy and safety of IR methylphenidate for preschoolers with ADHD (PATS). JAACAP 2006 (PMID 17023867)
